steps.d: Many tours stop first at this My Tho pagoda, with a giant white Buddha and a laughing Buddha in the gardens.
Cross the wide brown river past fish farms and the delta's islands.
Honey tea with kumquat; the guide lets people hold a frame of live bees.
Seasonal fruit at a garden house while local musicians play southern folk songs (don ca tai tu).
The highlight: a small rowing boat, steered by a local in a conical hat, glides down a narrow canal under water palms.
Watch coconut candy being cooked, cut and wrapped by hand, with free tasting.
Easy, flat bikes along shady lanes past orchards, stilt houses and small bridges.
Some tours swap the bikes for a short horse-cart ride or another small boat.
Then the ride back to Saigon, about 2 hours.
A short black-and-white film and a cutaway map of the three-level tunnel network.
A guide reveals a tiny camouflaged entrance in the leaf litter; anyone can try squeezing in for a photo.
Displays of the spike and swinging traps used against soldiers.
A US tank left where it was hit by a mine.
A stretch widened for visitors, about 100 m, with exits every 20 m or so. Hot, dark and low, so it's fine to skip.
See the smokeless kitchen and try steamed cassava dipped in peanut-sesame salt with tea.
An extra-cost range with wartime rifles; it's loud across the whole site.
Thailand's most sacred temple: a small jade Buddha high on a golden altar. No photos inside; shoes off.
The cloister around the temple is painted with 178 panels of the Thai Ramayana epic.
The gold-tiled Phra Si Rattana chedi and the towering demon guardians (yaksha) at the gates.
The royal throne hall: a European-style building topped with Thai roofs.
46 m long and covered in gold leaf, with mother-of-pearl soles.
Buy a cup of coins (about 20 THB) and drop one in each bowl along the wall for luck.
Tall chedis covered in coloured ceramic tiles, one for each of the first four kings.
Rows of gilded Buddhas and Chinese stone statues; much calmer than the palace.
From Tha Tien pier, about 5 THB and 3 minutes.
The tower is covered in broken porcelain flowers; climb the steep steps to the first terraces.
Shops by the gate rent traditional outfits for photos.

steps.t: Buddha head in the tree roots
steps.d: The famous stone head grown into a banyan tree. Crouch so heads stay lower than the Buddha's in photos.
Lines of seated statues damaged when Ayutthaya fell in 1767.
Walk among the collapsed towers of the old royal monastery.
The bell-shaped chedis lined up on the old royal palace grounds.
Next door: a working temple with one of Thailand's largest bronze Buddhas.
A tall prang ringed by smaller towers, on the river bank.
Rows of Buddha statues around the gallery walls.
The bricks glow orange in the late afternoon; best photos from across the lawn.

steps.t: Find a spot by the track
steps.d: Arrive 20 minutes early and stand in a shop doorway or a café by the rails.
A bell rings, then vendors pull back their umbrellas and move baskets seconds before the train.
It passes inches from the produce, then everything goes back as if nothing happened.
The train turns around at the station and leaves 30 to 40 minutes later, so it can be seen twice.
Old wooden shophouses, coffee shops and small stalls on both banks.
Grilled prawns, squid and noodles cooked on boats and handed up to the steps.
A short boat ride along the canal before dark, about 50 to 100 THB each.
About an hour along the Mae Klong river and canals.
Thousands blink in the trees along the banks; best on a dark, still night.
About 30,000 VND each way to the main gate.
A long covered walkway lined with 500 stone statues, each with a different face.
Home to a giant bronze bell, with views over the valley.
The main halls hold huge bronze Buddhas, the biggest about 100 tonnes.
A lift to the top for the view, at extra cost.
At the foot of the cliff by a small lotus pond.
Steps lead into a cave shrine, then out to the middle level.
The top level has a quiet view over the fields.
The main temple, with carved wooden halls and a stone dragon bed.
A smaller, quieter temple a short walk away.
About 200 steps up to the king's tomb, with a view over the valley.
Local women row flat bamboo boats across a mirror-calm lagoon.
The boat floats into small caves at the foot of the cliffs.
Rare Delacour's langurs sometimes sit on the rocks; the rower will point them out.
Pastel buildings, a clock tower and squares made for photos.
Two halves that almost meet over the sea; couples kiss at the gap at sunset.
Seating on the stands by the water opens about 20 minutes before.
A Vietnamese love story told with water screens, fountains, lasers and fire, about 30 minutes.
It usually ends with fireworks over the sea.
Paths past monkeys, flamingos, hippos and giraffes, many in open enclosures.
A bus drives through the big-animal zone with lions, tigers, bears and rhinos close by.
Short shows and giraffe or elephant feeding at set times.
A walk out over the sea, with the fishing boats moored alongside.
Pick crab, sea urchin or squid and have it cooked at a stilt restaurant.
Small shops sell local pearls and dried fish.
One of the island's whitest beaches, with calm, clear water.
Loungers at the beach clubs, free if you order food or drinks.
